lessons.title: Ein billigerer Becher: comparatives before a noun
lessons.goal: Put a comparative in front of a noun with the right ending: ein billigerer Becher, die bessere Idee, frischeres Gemüse.

grammar.point: A comparative in front of a noun takes the normal adjective ending after the -er: billig, billiger, ein billigerer Becher. After der, die, das the ending is -e or -en, after ein it shows the gender (-er, -e, -es), without an article it copies the missing article. mehr and weniger never take an ending. Irregular stems stay: besser, höher, näher, größer, älter.

mistake.wrong: Das ist ein billiger Becher als der Einwegbecher.
mistake.right: Das ist ein billigerer Becher als der Einwegbecher.
mistake.why: Comparative -er comes first, then the ending -er. billiger alone means cheap, not cheaper.

terms.meaning: the 'more' form of an adjective: billiger, besser, größer
the letters added to an adjective in front of a noun, such as -e, -en, -er, -es

cards.title: Before we start: from 'Der Becher ist billiger' to 'ein billigerer Becher'
cards.body: This chapter is called Umweltfreundlich?: good for the environment, or is it really? Mira works at Datenhafen and reads about start-ups that want less waste. You can already say Der Becher ist billiger. Today the comparison moves in front of a noun, and then it needs an ending as well.
steps: You already know: Der Mehrwegbecher ist billiger. and Ich suche einen neuen Becher.: comparing after sein, and adjective endings.
New today: both together: Ich suche einen billigeren Becher. and Es gibt eine bessere Idee.
By the end you can: put a comparative in front of a noun with the right ending, in the nominative, accusative and dative.

examples.de: Der Mehrwegbecher ist billiger.
examples.en: The reusable cup is cheaper.
examples.why: You know this: after sein the comparative stands alone.

examples.de: Ich suche einen billigeren Becher.
examples.en: I am looking for a cheaper cup.
examples.why: New today: comparative -er, then the ending -en for the accusative.

cards.more: Imagine an adjective as a little train. billig is one carriage. Add -er and the train is longer: billiger, cheaper. After sein the train simply stops there. But when a noun follows, German wants one more coupling: the ending you already know from ein neuer Becher. So the cheaper cup is billig plus er plus en. Two small pieces, one after the other. Nothing else is new, only the order.

cards.title: Coffee break at Datenhafen
cards.body: Mira and a colleague read about the start-up „Becherwerk“. In each line look for two things: a comparative like billiger, and what stands behind it. When a noun follows (Idee, Lösung), the comparative has an extra ending.
cards.lead: A short scene from the coffee break at Datenhafen. Read it once and notice the words that end in -er or -e in front of a noun. The next cards take them apart.

examples.de: Das ist eine bessere Idee als Einwegbecher.
examples.en: That is a better idea than disposable cups.

examples.de: Gibt es auch eine billigere Lösung?
examples.en: Is there also a cheaper solution?

examples.de: Wir brauchen einen leichteren Becher.
examples.en: We need a lighter cup.

deeper.text: Comparing a general kind of thing needs no article after als: besser als Einwegbecher. Comparing one particular thing does: als der Einwegbecher von gestern. Both are correct. The version without an article sounds more like a general statement, the version with it like a concrete choice.

example.de: Mehrwegbecher sind besser als Einwegbecher.
example.en: Reusable cups are better than disposable cups.

cards.more: Think of a café menu. One line says: Der Kaffee ist billiger. That is a statement about the coffee. Another line says: Ein billigerer Kaffee? Now cheaper is a label stuck on the thing itself, like a sticker on a cup. German stickers always come with an ending so that the whole group fits into its sentence. Read the lines aloud and listen for the three beats: billig, er, e.
steps: Mira: Schau mal, hier steht etwas über „Becherwerk“.
Kollegin: Ach ja, Mehrwegbecher für Cafés. Das ist eine bessere Idee als Einwegbecher.
Mira: Genau. Man zahlt einen Euro Pfand und bringt den Becher später zurück.
Kollegin: Gibt es auch eine billigere Lösung?
Mira: Vielleicht. Aber billiger ist nicht immer besser.
Kollegin: Stimmt. Ich nehme trotzdem einen leichteren Becher.

cards.title: Two jobs of the comparative
cards.body: After sein, werden or finden the comparative stands alone: billiger. In front of a noun it takes an ending too. Build it in two steps: first adjective plus -er, then the ending you already know from ein neuer Becher.
cards.lead: Cards one showed the comparative in two places. Now you see the difference side by side: alone after sein, or in front of a noun with a second ending.

examples.de: Dieser Becher ist billiger.
examples.en: This cup is cheaper.

examples.de: Das ist ein billigerer Becher.
examples.en: That is a cheaper cup.

examples.de: Leon kauft einen billigeren Becher.
examples.en: Leon buys a cheaper cup.

deeper.text: English adds -er or more and stops: a cheaper cup. German adds the comparative and then still the ending. Many learners leave out the second part and say ein billiger Becher. That sentence is correct German, but it means a cheap cup, not a cheaper one.

example.de: Das ist ein billiger Becher.
example.en: That is a cheap cup.

cards.more: Picture a sandwich. The bread slices are the comparative -er and the ending. billig is only the filling. If you have just one slice, you have a different sandwich: billiger alone is the comparative, billig plus er is the plain adjective with an ending. A cheaper cup needs both slices: billig, then er for more, then er, en or es for the noun. Check slice two whenever a noun follows.
steps: 1  Make the comparative: billig → billiger.
2  A noun right behind it? Add the ending you know from ein neuer Becher: ein billigerer Becher.

cards.title: After der, die, das
cards.body: After der, die, das and dieser the ending is -e or -en, exactly as in der neue Plan. Put it behind the comparative. -e stands in the nominative (all genders) and for die and das in the accusative. Everywhere else: -en.
cards.lead: You already know the endings after der-words from der neue Plan. Now only the comparative is added in front of them: besser plus e or en.

examples.de: Das ist der bessere Plan.
examples.en: That is the better plan.

examples.de: Mira liest den längeren Artikel.
examples.en: Mira reads the longer article.

examples.de: Wir arbeiten mit dem billigeren Konzept.
examples.en: We work with the cheaper concept.

deeper.text: Adjectives that end in -er or -el lose an e when an ending is added. teuer becomes teurer in the comparative, and with an ending der teurere Becher. dunkel becomes dunkler and then die dunklere Farbe. The e before the r or l drops out, so you never see teuerer.

example.de: Der teurere Becher hält länger.
example.en: The more expensive cup lasts longer.

cards.more: Forget the table and count: of the four cases, -e only appears three times in the singular (nominative of der, die, das) plus accusative of die and das. That is five spots. All the rest are -en. So the safe guess is -en, and you only need to remember the five -e spots. The comparative changes nothing about this guess: besser is just the new adjective.

cards.title: After ein, kein, mein
cards.body: After ein-words the adjective shows the gender: -er for der-nouns, -es for das-nouns. With a comparative this gives billigerer and billigeres: the first -er is the comparison, the second the ending. It looks odd but is regular.
cards.lead: Ein-words have no ending in some spots, so the adjective has to show the gender. With a comparative that gives a double -er, which you will meet here.

examples.de: Ich suche einen billigeren Becher.
examples.en: I am looking for a cheaper cup.

examples.de: Das ist ein billigeres Konzept.
examples.en: That is a cheaper concept.

examples.de: Hast du eine billigere Tasche?
examples.en: Do you have a cheaper bag?

deeper.text: In speech people often avoid the heavy ein teurerer Becher and use a relative clause from A2 instead: ein Becher, der teurer ist. Both are correct. The relative clause moves the comparative back after sein, where it needs no ending at all, so it is a handy escape when the double ending feels too long.

example.de: Ich suche einen Becher, der billiger ist.
example.en: I am looking for a cup that is cheaper.

cards.more: Say it aloud like a drum roll: bil-li-ge-rer Be-cher. The first er belongs to the comparison, the second marks a der-noun, just like the er in ein neuer Becher. Other genders sound simpler: eine billigere Tasche, ein billigeres Konzept. So the odd-looking double only happens with der-nouns in the nominative. In the accusative it turns into billigeren, which sounds smoother. Try it with three cups of your own and say each one slowly.

cards.title: Irregular stems before a noun
cards.body: Some comparatives change their stem: gut → besser, hoch → höher (the c disappears), nah → näher, groß → größer, alt → älter. They take the usual ending: der höhere Preis. mehr and weniger never take an ending: mehr Müll, weniger Plastik.
cards.lead: You know the odd comparatives from A2: besser, höher, näher. Now they go in front of nouns and take endings, with one exception: mehr and weniger.

examples.de: Es gibt weniger Plastik im Meer.
examples.en: There is less plastic in the sea.

examples.de: Das ist das größere Problem.
examples.en: That is the bigger problem.

examples.de: Der nähere Weg führt durch den Park.
examples.en: The nearer path leads through the park.

deeper.text: andere looks like a comparative because it ends in -er, but it is an ordinary adjective: ein anderer Becher means a different cup. The -er is just the masculine ending. If you cannot put als behind it and mean more of something, it is no comparative. Compare ein besserer Becher, a cup that is better.

example.de: Ich nehme einen anderen Becher.
example.en: I will take a different cup.

cards.more: Think of a few rebels in a class. gut will not say gut-er, it says besser. hoch loses its c and turns into höher, as if it had lost a button. mehr and weniger are the two who never wear a coat: no endings, ever. Everyone else obeys the usual rules. Learn the rebels as small pairs and you are safe: gut-besser, hoch-höher, nah-näher, groß-größer, alt-älter.

cards.title: Comparing start-ups
cards.body: Without an article, the adjective takes the ending of the missing article: frischeres Gemüse (das), größere Städte (die), mit größerem Erfolg (dem). Use this to compare the start-ups „Gemüsekiste Spree“ and „Zweite Runde“.
cards.lead: Cards three and four had an article. The last pattern has none, as in frischeres Gemüse. The adjective then does the work of the article alone.

examples.de: „Gemüsekiste Spree“ bringt frischeres Gemüse als der Supermarkt.
examples.en: „Gemüsekiste Spree“ brings fresher vegetables than the supermarket.

examples.de: „Zweite Runde“ hat eine größere Auswahl.
examples.en: „Zweite Runde“ has a bigger selection.

examples.de: In größeren Städten gibt es mehr Cafés.
examples.en: In bigger cities there are more cafés.

deeper.text: immer plus a comparative means more and more: immer mehr, immer größer, immer billiger. In front of a noun the adjective keeps its ending: immer größere Städte. This is how people talk about trends, for example how many cafés offer reusable cups.

example.de: Immer mehr Cafés haben Mehrwegbecher.
example.en: More and more cafés have reusable cups.

cards.more: Imagine the article is an invisible friend. When it is missing, the adjective stands in its shoes and borrows its ending. Das Gemüse would be das, so the adjective says es: frischeres Gemüse. Die Städte would be die, so: größere Städte. mit dem Erfolg would be dem, so: mit größerem Erfolg. If you know the article, you know the ending: just take the last letters of the invisible article.

lessons.title: Die beste Idee: superlatives before a noun
lessons.goal: Name the winner in front of a noun with the right ending: der billigste Becher, mit der besten Idee. Choose between am billigsten and der billigste.

grammar.point: A superlative in front of a noun is adjective + st + the normal ending, almost always with der, die or das: der billigste Becher, den besten Plan. After t, d, s, ß, z or sch the stem adds an e: der älteste, die interessanteste; groß is an exception: die größte. After sein without a noun use am ... -sten, before a noun only der ... -ste, never am.

mistake.wrong: Das ist die am besten Idee.
mistake.why: Before a noun there is no am: just the article, the superlative stem and the ending.

terms.meaning: the 'most' form of an adjective: billigst-, best-, größt-
the adjective without an ending, for example billigst- in der billigste Becher

cards.title: Before we start: from 'am besten' to 'die beste Idee'
cards.body: Three start-ups, one winner: which idea is the best? To name a winner you need the superlative. You already say Diese Idee ist am besten. Today the superlative stands in front of a noun: die beste Idee, das günstigste Angebot. It works like the comparative from the last lesson.
steps: You already know: Diese Idee ist am besten. and Der Becher ist am billigsten.: the superlative after sein.
New today: Das ist die beste Idee. and Wir nehmen das günstigste Angebot.: the superlative in front of a noun.
By the end you can: name the winner with the right ending, and choose between am billigsten and der billigste.

examples.de: Diese Idee ist am besten.
examples.en: This idea is best.
examples.why: You know this: after sein, no noun, am ... -sten.

examples.de: Das ist die beste Idee.
examples.en: That is the best idea.
examples.why: New today: article, superlative, ending, noun.

cards.more: A race has a winner. After sein you say who is fastest: Er ist am schnellsten. When you want to put a name tag on the winner, you say: Er ist der schnellste Läufer. The tag always starts with der, die or das, because there is only one winner. Then comes the superlative stem and an ending you already know. That is all: the winner is the one with the article.

cards.title: Which start-up wins?
cards.body: The WG votes for the best of three ideas. In every line the superlative stands in front of a noun and ends in -ste. Spot the -ste and the article before it.
cards.lead: The WG argues over which start-up wins. Read the lines once and spot the words that end in -ste before a noun. The next cards build the rule.

examples.de: „Zweite Runde“ hat die größte Auswahl.
examples.en: „Zweite Runde“ has the biggest selection.

examples.de: Das ist die einfachste Lösung.
examples.en: That is the simplest solution.

examples.de: „Gemüsekiste Spree“ hat das frischeste Gemüse.
examples.en: „Gemüsekiste Spree“ has the freshest vegetables.

deeper.text: The article in front of a superlative is not optional. Wir nehmen günstigste Angebot is wrong, it must be das günstigste Angebot. Only one thing can be the cheapest, so German points at it with der, die or das. You can swap the article for dieser or jeder, but never leave it out.

example.de: Wir nehmen das günstigste Angebot.
example.en: We take the cheapest offer.

cards.more: Picture a podium with three steps. On the top step stands one idea. A sign hangs above it: die beste. The sign always has the little word der, die or das on it, because it points at exactly one winner. Underneath the sign the idea has its name: Idee. The WG scene lets you read the signs one by one. Look for the -ste at the end of each sign.
steps: Mira: Wir müssen entscheiden, welche Idee die beste ist.
Ben: „Zweite Runde“ hat die größte Auswahl. Das ist die einfachste Lösung für alte Kleidung.
Anna: Aber „Becherwerk“ ist die umweltfreundlichste Idee. Mit einem Mehrwegbecher braucht man viel weniger Einwegbecher.
Leon: Und „Gemüsekiste Spree“ hat das frischeste Gemüse!
Ben: Das stimmt. Aber die billigste Lösung ist das nicht.
Mira: Okay, drei gute Ideen. Wer stimmt für welche?

cards.title: Build it: adjective + st + ending
cards.body: Make the superlative stem first: billig → billigst. Then add the ending: der billigste Becher, die billigste Tasche, das billigste Angebot. In the plural it is -en: die billigsten Becher. A superlative in front of a noun almost always has der, die or das.
cards.lead: Last lesson you built the comparative with -er. Now the same two steps with -st: first the superlative stem, then the ending after der, die or das.

examples.de: Das ist der billigste Becher.
examples.en: That is the cheapest cup.

examples.de: Sie haben die billigsten Becher der Stadt.
examples.en: They have the cheapest cups in the city.

examples.de: Ich nehme das leichteste Angebot.
examples.en: I take the easiest offer.

deeper.text: English never puts an ending on the cheapest. German always does when a noun follows, and the ending changes with the case: der billigste Becher, den billigsten Becher. That is why you must say the article first: it tells you which ending belongs. Learn the pair der billigste, den billigsten together.

example.de: Ich kaufe den billigsten Becher.
example.en: I buy the cheapest cup.

cards.more: Build a staircase of three steps. Step one: the plain word, billig. Step two: add -st, and you have the champion, billigst. Step three: put the champion in its seat and give it the seat belt, the ending: der billigste Becher. Nobody gets on the stage without the belt. When you see a noun after a superlative, always check for step three. Say it aloud: billig, billigst, der billigste.
steps: 1  Take the adjective: billig.
2  Add -st: billigst.
3  Add the ending after der, die or das: der billigste Becher, die billigsten Becher.

cards.title: All cases with the superlative
cards.body: After der, die, das the superlative takes the same endings as the comparative did in the last lesson: -e or -en. -e is for the nominative and for die and das in the accusative. Everywhere else the ending is -en.
cards.lead: You know these endings already from der neue Plan and from lesson one. Here is the whole table for the best idea, in every case.

examples.de: Ben hat die beste Idee.
examples.en: Ben has the best idea.

examples.de: Wir wählen den besten Plan.
examples.en: We choose the best plan.

examples.de: Mit der besten Idee gewinnt das Team.
examples.en: With the best idea the team wins.

deeper.text: After mein, dein, unser the superlative takes the endings of ein: -er, -e, -es. So you say mein bester Freund, meine beste Freundin and unser bestes Konzept. The article word changes, but the superlative stem stays the same. This is the usual pattern for best friends and favourites.

example.de: Mira ist meine beste Kollegin.
example.en: Mira is my best colleague.

cards.more: You have seen this grid before, so only one question is left: which seat is the idea sitting in? The subject sits in the nominative, the thing that is chosen sits in the accusative, and anything after mit sits in the dative. For each seat copy the ending from the grid: -e on the three easy seats, -en on all the rest. The grid for best is the same as the grid for better, minus the -er.

cards.title: -este and irregular forms
cards.body: Adjectives ending in t, d, s, ß, z or sch add -est: älteste, kürzeste, heißeste, interessanteste, frischeste. groß is an exception: die größte. Some are irregular: beste, meisten, höchste, nächste.
cards.lead: Some superlative stems would be hard to say. This card shows when you need the extra e, and lists the irregular ones you know from A2.

examples.de: Das war der heißeste Tag im Jahr.
examples.en: That was the hottest day of the year.

examples.de: Mira hat die interessanteste Idee.
examples.en: Mira has the most interesting idea.

examples.de: Wo ist der nächste Supermarkt?
examples.en: Where is the nearest supermarket?

deeper.text: die meisten means most and needs its article: Die meisten Leute kaufen im Supermarkt ein. A sentence like Meiste Leute is wrong. Notice also that meisten is plural here: most people. With a singular noun you rather say am meisten or the most of something.

example.de: Die meisten Leute kaufen im Supermarkt ein.
example.en: Most people shop at the supermarket.

cards.more: Say the words slowly. älteste has three clear syllables: äl-te-ste. If you drop the e you get älteste with a crunchy -tst, which is hard to say. So German adds a small helper e after t, d, s, ß, z or sch: älteste, heißeste. groß is a rebel because ß is followed by t without trouble: größte. Listen for the extra e and you will remember when it is needed.

cards.title: am billigsten or der billigste?
cards.body: After sein with no noun you have two choices: am billigsten (the cup is most cheap) or der billigste (noun left out). Before a noun there is only one: der billigste Becher. Never write am before a noun.
cards.lead: Now two ways of saying the same thing meet. This card sorts out when to use am ... -sten and when to use der ... -ste.

examples.de: Dieser Becher ist am billigsten.
examples.en: This cup is the cheapest.

examples.de: Das ist der billigste Becher.
examples.en: That is the cheapest cup.

examples.de: Der Becher ist der billigste.
examples.en: The cup is the cheapest one.

deeper.text: In German you can compare in pairs: je mehr, desto besser. Je mehr Leute mitmachen, desto besser. The more people take part, the better. You may read and hear this pattern now. You do not need to use it yet, because it follows its own word-order rules and you meet it again later.

example.de: Je mehr Leute mitmachen, desto besser.
example.en: The more people join in, the better.

cards.more: Think of a shop shelf. If the shelf has no label, you shout: Dieser ist am billigsten! The am stands in for a noun that is missing. If the label names the product, you say: Das ist der billigste Becher. There is no am anymore, because the noun is on the label. If the noun is left out but the label is still there, you keep der and the ending: Der Becher ist der billigste.

cards.title: The Pfand bottle check
cards.body: A real-life comparison: which bottle is best? The glass bottle is the heaviest, but the reusable bottle is the most environmentally friendly. Use the superlative with an article, and in Germany think of Pfand.
cards.lead: You know how to name a winner. Now use it in a real comparison from the supermarket: the Pfand bottle, the one-way bottle and the can.

examples.de: Für eine Einwegflasche zahlt man 25 Cent Pfand.
examples.en: For a one-way bottle you pay 25 cents deposit.

examples.de: Die Mehrwegflasche kostet meistens acht oder fünfzehn Cent Pfand.
examples.en: The reusable bottle usually costs eight or fifteen cents deposit.

examples.de: An der Rückgabe bekommt man einen Pfandbon.
examples.en: At the return machine you get a deposit slip.

deeper.text: Das Pfand is the money, das Leergut is the empty bottles you carry back. Many people keep Leergut in a crate or bag at home. The rules are different in Austria and Switzerland, so check there before you return a bottle. In Germany you get a Pfandbon, which you hand over at the till.

example.de: Das Leergut bringe ich am Samstag zurück.
example.en: I bring the empties back on Saturday.

cards.more: Imagine a bottle race with three runners. The glass bottle is strong but heavy. The can is light but needs a lot of energy to produce. The reusable bottle runs again and again. For the environment the reusable bottle is the winner, and you can say so with the sign die umweltfreundlichste. The deposit is the small reward that makes people bring bottles back. Check the sentence below for the sign.

lessons.title: Ideen für eine grünere Straße
lessons.goal: Present an idea, ask for opinions, react politely and choose the best idea, using the comparatives and superlatives from lessons one and two.

grammar.point: Present ideas with Ich hätte da eine Idee, Wie wäre es mit + dative, Man könnte … and Was wäre, wenn wir …? Ask with Was hältst du davon? or Was hältst du von + dative? and react with Gute Idee!, Die Idee gefällt mir, weil … or Ich weiß nicht so recht. Compare with comparatives and superlatives before nouns. mit always takes the dative.
grammar.oneLine: Wie wäre es mit einer Fahrradstraße?

mistake.wrong: Wie wäre es mit eine Fahrradstraße?
mistake.right: Wie wäre es mit einer Fahrradstraße?
mistake.why: mit always takes the dative: einer for a die-noun.

terms.meaning: the case after mit and von: einem, einer, dem, der
two nouns in one word; the last part gives the article: die Fahrradstraße

cards.title: Before we start: from 'Ich habe eine Idee' to 'Wie wäre es mit einer Fahrradstraße?'
cards.body: Leon dreams of a greener street. To talk about ideas you need more than grammar: you need phrases for presenting an idea, asking what others think and answering politely. This lesson teaches no new grammar. You use the comparatives, superlatives and dream forms you already have.
steps: You already know: Man könnte das Dach begrünen. and Wie wäre es mit einem Grillfest?: suggestions with könnte and wäre.
New today: Ich hätte da eine Idee: … and Was hältst du davon?: phrases to present an idea and ask for opinions.
By the end you can: present an idea, ask what others think, react politely and say which idea is the best.

examples.de: Man könnte das Dach begrünen.
examples.en: You could plant the roof with greenery.
examples.why: You know this: a suggestion with könnte.

examples.de: Ich hätte da eine Idee: eine Fahrradstraße.
examples.en: I have an idea: a bike street.
examples.why: New today: a modest way to start your idea.

cards.more: Think of a meeting as a small game with four moves. First you put an idea on the table. Then you ask: what do you think? Then somebody answers, yes, maybe or no. At the end you pick the best idea. Each move has a few ready-made phrases in German. You can learn them like game pieces and then reuse them in every discussion, in German class or at work.

cards.title: Leon's dream street
cards.body: Leon, Mira, Anna and Ben imagine a greener street. Read the six lines once and notice how they present ideas: mehr Bäume, eine Fahrradstraße, ein Lastenrad für alle, ein Gründach.
cards.lead: Leon tells the WG his dream. Read it once and notice the four ideas, and the dream forms hätten, könnte, wäre that frame them.

examples.de: Wir hätten mehr Bäume und weniger Autos.
examples.en: We would have more trees and fewer cars.

examples.de: Wie wäre es mit einer Fahrradstraße?
examples.en: How about a bike street?

examples.de: Man könnte das Dach begrünen.
examples.en: You could plant the roof with greenery.

deeper.text: A dream sentence often has a signal that you are not talking about facts: stell dir vor (imagine), vielleicht, wäre, hätte. Leon starts with stell dir vor. That small phrase changes the whole mood and tells everyone that a dream follows. It works for ideas in a meeting too.

example.de: Stell dir vor, unsere Straße wäre grüner.
example.en: Imagine our street were greener.

cards.more: Imagine you are drawing a street on a piece of paper. First the trees, then the bike lane, then the cargo bike under a roof. Leon does the same, but with words. Every line adds one more element to the picture. You do not have to know every word at the first reading: draw the picture in your head and then read it again for the German.
steps: Leon: Stell dir vor, unsere Straße wäre grüner.
Leon: Wir hätten mehr Bäume und weniger Autos.
Mira: Und wo würden die Autos parken?
Leon: Gar nicht. Wie wäre es mit einer Fahrradstraße?
Anna: Ein Lastenrad für alle wäre auch praktisch.
Ben: Man könnte auch das Dach begrünen.

cards.title: Presenting an idea
cards.body: Four phrases to put an idea on the table: Ich hätte da eine Idee: … / Wie wäre es mit + dative? / Man könnte … / Was wäre, wenn wir …? Choose one and finish it with your idea.
cards.lead: After the dream, the tools. Here are four phrases you can use to present an idea politely, and you know three of them already.

examples.de: Ich hätte da eine Idee: einen Stadtgarten.
examples.en: I have an idea: an urban garden.

examples.de: Wie wäre es mit einem Lastenrad?
examples.en: How about a cargo bike?

examples.de: Was wäre, wenn wir eine Fahrradstraße hätten?
examples.en: What if we had a bike street?

deeper.text: In Ich hätte da eine Idee the little word da is not a place. It is a softener: it makes the sentence sound modest, as if you were saying, well, I might have one. Native speakers use it to avoid sounding bossy. Without it the sentence is still correct, but it sounds harder.

example.de: Ich hätte da noch eine Idee.
example.en: I have another idea.

cards.more: Think of a market stall. You do not shout your offer, you lay it out and invite people to look. Ich hätte da eine Idee lays it out. Wie wäre es mit … asks if somebody would like it. Man könnte … says it quietly and lets others decide. Was wäre, wenn … is a thought experiment. Pick the phrase that fits your mood, and always finish with your idea.

rows: Ich hätte da eine Idee: ein Gründach.
Wie wäre es mit einem Stadtgarten?
Was wäre, wenn wir autofrei wären?

cards.title: Asking and reacting
cards.body: Ask for opinions with Was hältst du davon? or Was meinst du dazu? halten von + dative means to think of: Was hältst du von einer Fahrradstraße? Answer with Gute Idee!, Die Idee gefällt mir, weil … or Das finde ich nicht so gut, weil …
cards.lead: An idea needs an answer. This card gives you ways to ask what people think, and ways to say yes, maybe or no without sounding rude.

examples.de: Was hältst du von einer Fahrradstraße?
examples.en: What do you think of a bike street?

examples.de: Die Idee gefällt mir, weil sie einfach ist.
examples.en: I like the idea because it is simple.

examples.de: Das finde ich nicht so gut, weil es zu teuer ist.
examples.en: I do not find that so good because it is too expensive.

deeper.text: Ich weiß nicht so recht is the polite German no. It does not say that the idea is bad, it says that you are not convinced yet. Often a reason follows. This is how Germans avoid saying nein directly in a meeting, especially with people they respect.

example.de: Ich weiß nicht so recht, ob das klappt.
example.en: I am not so sure whether that will work.

cards.more: Imagine a traffic light for ideas. Green: Gute Idee! or Die Idee gefällt mir. Yellow: Ich weiß nicht so recht. Red: Das finde ich nicht so gut. After yellow or red you almost always give a reason with weil, so the other person can reply. The question Was hältst du davon? is the button you press to turn the light on. Say it with a friendly voice.

rows: Was hältst du davon? / Was meinst du dazu? / Was hältst du von + Dativ?
Gute Idee! / Die Idee gefällt mir, weil …
Das finde ich nicht so gut, weil …

cards.title: Comparing ideas
cards.body: To say which idea is better, use the comparatives and superlatives you have just learned. A comparative before a noun needs an ending, a superlative needs der, die or das: eine praktischere Lösung, die einfachste Idee.
cards.lead: Now the two lessons work together: you compare ideas with comparatives and name the winner with a superlative, in front of nouns.

examples.de: Ein Lastenrad ist eine praktischere Lösung als ein zweites Auto.
examples.en: A cargo bike is a more practical solution than a second car.

examples.de: Die einfachste Idee ist oft die beste.
examples.en: The simplest idea is often the best.

examples.de: Für Kinder ist eine Fahrradstraße die sicherste Lösung.
examples.en: For children a bike street is the safest solution.

deeper.text: A good argument links a comparison with a reason. Use weil after the judgement or deshalb after the reason. Ich finde das Lastenrad besser, weil es weniger kostet. Or: Es kostet weniger, deshalb ist es die bessere Lösung. Both orders work, and deshalb puts the verb right after it.

example.de: Es kostet weniger, deshalb ist es die bessere Lösung.
example.en: It costs less, therefore it is the better solution.

cards.more: Think of a boxing ring, with one champion at the end. Each comparative is a round: is the cargo bike more practical than a car? Yes, round one. Is the bike street safer than the old street? Yes, round two. At the end the referee raises one arm and says the superlative: die einfachste Idee, die beste Lösung. Use the rounds in your next discussion and finish with the champion.

cards.title: Green city words in use
cards.body: Every idea has an advantage. Write it as idea + advantage: Fahrradstraße → weniger Verkehr, Gründach → kühlere Häuser, Carsharing → weniger Autos. Use these in short sentences with a comparative.
cards.lead: Ideas are only convincing with an advantage. This card gives you the green city words as pairs, so each idea comes with its reason.

examples.de: Eine Fahrradstraße bringt weniger Verkehr.
examples.en: A bike street brings less traffic.

examples.de: Ein Gründach macht die Häuser im Sommer kühler.
examples.en: A green roof makes the houses cooler in summer.

examples.de: Carsharing bedeutet weniger Autos in der Stadt.
examples.en: Car sharing means fewer cars in the city.

deeper.text: A compound noun takes the article of its last part: das Dach gives das Gründach, die Straße gives die Fahrradstraße, der Garten gives der Stadtgarten. So look at the last word to know the gender. You will see this again in a later lesson in the chapter about word families.

example.de: Die Fahrradstraße ist neu.
example.en: The bike street is new.

cards.more: Picture a seesaw. On the left sits the idea, on the right sits its advantage. A good idea has a heavy advantage. Fahrradstraße is the idea; weniger Verkehr is the weight. Gründach is the idea; kühlere Häuser is the weight. If you can name the weight, you can defend the idea. Try to make one seesaw for every idea you propose, and say it aloud to a friend before the meeting.

cards.title: Berlin without a car
cards.body: Many Berliners have no car. They use the bike, the U-Bahn or Carsharing. This is why ideas like a cargo bike or a bike street fit well in the city.
cards.lead: Last, a look at real life. Why do ideas about bikes and car sharing fit a city like Berlin? A few general facts help you to argue.

examples.de: Viele Berliner haben kein Auto.
examples.en: Many Berliners have no car.

examples.de: Man fährt mit dem Fahrrad oder mit der U-Bahn.
examples.en: You travel by bike or by U-Bahn.

examples.de: Mit Carsharing braucht man kein eigenes Auto.
examples.en: With car sharing you do not need a car of your own.

deeper.text: In many cities you can borrow cargo bikes, often from clubs or neighbourhood houses, and often for little or no money. ausleihen means to borrow. This is why a Lastenrad for everybody is a realistic idea, not only a dream. Compare A2: leihen can mean both to lend and to borrow, while ausleihen is clearly to borrow.

example.de: Wir können ein Lastenrad ausleihen.
example.en: We can borrow a cargo bike.

cards.more: A city is a big shared house. In a flat nobody owns a washing machine each, you share one. In a city, many people share bikes, trains and cars in the same way. In Berlin the sharing is easy because the U-Bahn goes everywhere. That is a reason for a street with fewer cars. It is not the whole story, but it gives your ideas a base.

lessons.title: Um weniger Müll zu produzieren: um … zu
lessons.goal: Say the goal of an action with Wozu? and um … zu + infinitive, also with separable verbs, and start the sentence with the um-part.

grammar.point: Wozu? asks for the goal of an action. The answer is um + the goal + zu + infinitive at the end: Ich fahre Rad, um Geld zu sparen. The person of the main sentence does both things, so there is no second subject. With a separable verb zu goes inside (wegzuwerfen). The um-part can also come first: then the verb follows right after the comma.

mistake.right: Ich kaufe auf dem Markt ein, um Plastik zu vermeiden.
mistake.why: After um there is no subject and no conjugated verb: use zu + infinitive at the end.

terms.meaning: what you want to reach with an action: Wozu? – Um … zu …

cards.title: Before we start: from 'Ich habe Lust, … zu …' to 'Ich kaufe ein, um …'
cards.body: Chapter 5 asks: is it really good for the environment? The WG wants to find out. Mira, Ben, Anna and Leon decide to produce less rubbish. You can already say what you plan: Wir haben vor, weniger Müll zu produzieren. Today you add the goal of an action: what you do something for.
steps: You already know: Wir haben vor, weniger Müll zu produzieren.: a plan with zu + infinitive from B1 chapter 1.
New today: Wir nehmen Stofftaschen mit, um Plastik zu vermeiden.: um … zu names the goal of an action.
By the end you can: answer Wozu? with um … zu, use it with separable verbs, and start a sentence with the um-part.

examples.de: Wir haben vor, weniger Müll zu produzieren.
examples.en: We plan to produce less rubbish.
examples.why: You know this: zu + infinitive after a plan.

examples.de: Wir nehmen Stofftaschen mit, um Plastik zu vermeiden.
examples.en: We take cloth bags along in order to avoid plastic.
examples.why: New today: um … zu names the goal.

cards.more: Think of a shopping list with a reason written behind every item. Stofftaschen: um Plastik zu vermeiden. Brotdose: um Verpackung zu sparen. The item is the action, the reason after um is the goal. In German both parts belong to one sentence, joined by a comma. The little word zu travels with you from chapter 1 of B1: it still stands in front of the infinitive. Only the opener um is new.

cards.title: The WG plan: Wozu brauchen wir das?
cards.body: Sunday in the WG kitchen. Mira has made a list of things to change. Ben asks what each thing is for. Look at the question Wozu? and at the answers: they start with um and end with zu + infinitive.
cards.lead: Before the rule, a scene. The four flatmates plan their month with less rubbish. Spot the question word Wozu? and the um … zu answers; the next cards take the pattern apart step by step.

examples.de: Wozu brauchen wir eine Brotdose?
examples.en: What do we need a lunch box for?

examples.de: Um weniger Verpackung wegzuwerfen.
examples.en: To throw away less packaging.

examples.de: Wir nehmen Stofftaschen mit, um Plastiktüten zu vermeiden.
examples.en: We take cloth bags along to avoid plastic bags.

deeper.text: Wozu? and Wofür? are close. Wozu asks for a goal, and the answer is um … zu. Wofür asks what a thing is used for, and the answer is für + noun. You know wofür from the wo-words in A2. In everyday speech both questions are very common, and people mix them without any trouble.

example.de: Wofür brauchst du die Dose?
example.en: What do you need the box for? – For my bread.

cards.more: Imagine each answer in the dialogue as a small label on a tool. The tool is the action: Stofftaschen mitnehmen. The label tells you its purpose: um Plastiktüten zu vermeiden. Ben asks Wozu? and reads the label aloud. Notice who acts: Anna carries the bags and Anna avoids the plastic, so one person does both. That is the secret of um … zu. Cover the label and the main sentence still works alone: the um-part is an extra.
steps: Mira: Wir wollen weniger Müll produzieren. Ich habe eine Liste gemacht.
Ben: Gut! Wozu brauchen wir eine Brotdose?
Mira: Um weniger Verpackung wegzuwerfen. Wir nehmen das Frühstück mit.
Anna: Und ich nehme Stofftaschen mit, um Plastiktüten zu vermeiden.
Leon: Ich trinke nur noch Leitungswasser, um Geld zu sparen.
Ben: Und ich kaufe auf dem Markt ein, um Plastik zu vermeiden.

cards.title: Build it: the goal at the end
cards.body: A main sentence says what you do. Then come a comma, um, and the goal with zu + infinitive at the end. The word zu stands right before the infinitive. You write no second subject.
cards.lead: All the answers in the scene had the same shape. Here you build that shape yourself in four short moves, starting from a normal main sentence that you already control.

examples.de: Ich fahre Rad, um Geld zu sparen.
examples.en: I ride a bike in order to save money.

examples.de: Leon kocht Suppe, um Reste zu verwenden.
examples.en: Leon cooks soup in order to use up leftovers.

examples.de: Anna trennt den Müll, um die Umwelt zu schützen.
examples.en: Anna separates the waste in order to protect the environment.

deeper.text: After um you never write a subject or a conjugated verb. The person in the main sentence does both things, so um … zu always needs the same person. Ich fahre Rad, um ich fit zu bleiben is wrong, because ich is already the subject. If another person gets the benefit, you need a different word, and you will meet it in the next lesson.

example.de: Ben kocht Suppe, um Geld zu sparen.
example.en: Ben cooks soup in order to save money.

cards.more: Picture a train. The main sentence is the engine with its driver. The um … zu part is one wagon hooked on behind, with the comma as the coupling. A wagon has no driver of its own: the driver of the engine runs the whole train. That is why there is no subject after um. The word zu sits like a signpost before the last stop, the infinitive. Build the engine first, then couple the wagon.
steps: Say what you do: Ich fahre Rad.
Add a comma and um: Ich fahre Rad, um …
Add the goal: the object first, the infinitive last: … um Geld zu sparen.
Put zu right before the infinitive: zu sparen, zu trennen, zu haben.

cards.title: Separable verbs: zu goes inside
cards.body: With a separable verb, zu goes between the prefix and the verb, and you write one word: wegwerfen becomes wegzuwerfen. You know this from B1 chapter 1. The word still stands at the end of the um-part.
cards.lead: Many everyday waste verbs are separable: wegwerfen, einkaufen, mitnehmen. Here you see where zu goes with them, so that you can say the goal of these actions correctly too.

examples.de: Ich nutze Mehrwegflaschen, um weniger wegzuwerfen.
examples.en: I use returnable bottles in order to throw away less.

examples.de: Wir gehen auf den Markt, um frisch einzukaufen.
examples.en: We go to the market in order to shop fresh.

examples.de: Mira packt eine Brotdose ein, um ihr Mittagessen mitzunehmen.
examples.en: Mira packs a lunch box in order to take her lunch along.

deeper.text: Verbs with an inseparable prefix never split, so zu stays in front: zu vermeiden, zu bekommen, zu entsorgen. The same goes for verbs without a prefix, such as zu sparen, and for verbs ending in -ieren or -eln, such as zu recyceln. A quick test: if the verb splits in a main sentence (Ich werfe es weg), zu goes inside; if it does not, zu goes in front.

example.de: Wir sammeln Papier, um es zu recyceln.
example.en: We collect paper in order to recycle it.

cards.more: Think of a separable verb as a two-part toy. In a main sentence the parts are apart: Ich werfe die Flasche weg. In the um … zu part the toy is clicked together again, and zu sits in the click like a small connector: weg-zu-werfen. Ask yourself one question: does this verb come apart in a main sentence? If yes, put zu between the two parts and write one word. Practise with mitnehmen: mitzunehmen.

rows: Wir kochen kleinere Portionen, um weniger wegzuwerfen.
Wir gehen auf den Markt, um frisch einzukaufen.
Ich habe eine Dose, um Reste mitzunehmen.
Wir treffen uns, um den Hof aufzuräumen.

cards.title: Wozu? or Warum?
cards.body: Warum? asks for a reason that already exists: the answer uses weil. Wozu? asks for a goal you want to reach: the answer uses um … zu. A quick test: if you can say in order to in English, use um … zu.
cards.lead: Both questions mean why in English, and that is the trap. Here you learn how to tell a reason from a goal, so that you pick weil or um … zu without having to think twice.

examples.de: Ich fahre Rad, weil es schnell ist.
examples.en: I ride a bike because it is fast.

examples.de: Ich fahre Rad, um fit zu bleiben.
examples.en: I ride a bike in order to stay fit.

examples.de: Ben spart Geld, um im Sommer nach Madrid zu fliegen.
examples.en: Ben saves money in order to fly to Madrid in the summer.

deeper.text: English often hides the um: I came to help. German needs it: Ich bin gekommen, um zu helfen. The form Ich bin gekommen zu helfen is not standard German. When there is no object, zu stands directly after um: um zu helfen, um zu lernen, um zu arbeiten. So every time English says to + verb for a goal, think um … zu.

example.de: Ich bin gekommen, um zu helfen.
example.en: I have come to help.

cards.more: Think of two questions at a door. Warum? looks backwards: what caused this? The answer with weil states a fact that already holds: Ich fahre Rad, weil es schnell ist. Wozu? looks forwards: what do you want to reach afterwards? The answer with um … zu names a target: Ich fahre Rad, um fit zu bleiben. If you can say because in English, use weil. If you can say in order to, use um … zu.

rows: the reason: it is like this
Ich fahre Rad, weil es schnell ist.
Ich fahre Rad, um fit zu bleiben.

cards.title: The um-part first
cards.body: The um-part can open the sentence. It fills position 1, so the verb follows directly after the comma and the subject comes after the verb. The meaning stays the same, but the goal comes first and gets more weight.
cards.lead: So far the goal stood at the end. In speech and in writing you often put it first. This card shows what happens to the word order when you do, and how to keep the verb in place.

examples.de: Um Müll zu vermeiden, kaufen wir auf dem Markt ein.
examples.en: To avoid rubbish, we shop at the market.

examples.de: Um Geld zu sparen, trinkt Leon Leitungswasser.
examples.en: To save money, Leon drinks tap water.

examples.de: Um weniger wegzuwerfen, planen wir jeden Sonntag das Essen.
examples.en: To throw away less, we plan the food every Sunday.

deeper.text: A close relative is ohne … zu, which means without doing something: Er geht, ohne das Licht auszuschalten. It has the same shape as um … zu, with ohne in the place of um. You will meet it in texts about habits, so just recognise it. You do not have to use it yet.

example.de: Er geht, ohne das Licht auszuschalten.
example.en: He leaves without switching off the light.

cards.more: Imagine the sentence as a seesaw. On one side sits the goal, Um Müll zu vermeiden, on the other side the main sentence, kaufen wir auf dem Markt ein. The comma is the pivot in the middle. Because the whole goal sits in position 1, the verb must come second, just as after Morgen or Heute. Count the goal as one block, then the verb, then the subject. That is the same rule as in every German main sentence.

cards.title: Short answers with um … zu
cards.body: In speech you can answer Wozu? with the um-part alone. It is a complete and natural answer. The first part is simply left out, because the question has already said it.
cards.lead: In real talk nobody repeats the whole sentence. The WG fridge list is full of short questions, and the answers are only the goal. This card shows how short answers sound and why they work.

examples.de: Um mein Brot mitzunehmen.
examples.en: To take my bread along.

examples.de: Um frisches Gemüse zu kaufen.
examples.en: To buy fresh vegetables.

examples.de: Um in Berlin zu arbeiten.
examples.en: To work in Berlin.

deeper.text: Wozu? can also stand alone as a reaction: Wozu das denn? means What is that for? or even Why on earth? It often sounds a little critical, as if the speaker doubts that the thing is useful. A friendly question therefore needs a fuller form, such as Wozu brauchst du das?

example.de: Wozu das denn?
example.en: What is that for, anyway?

cards.more: Think of a ping-pong rally. The question is the serve, and the short answer is the return. A return does not repeat the serve; it only brings the ball back with the new information. That new information is the goal: um … zu. If the question already contains the subject and the verb, you need nothing more. The whole um-part is the answer. In writing, add the first part, so that the sentence stands alone.

rows: Wozu gehst du auf den Markt?

lessons.title: Damit weniger im Müll landet: damit
lessons.goal: Give a goal for another person or thing with damit, choose between um … zu and damit, and keep modal verbs out of the damit-clause.

grammar.point: damit introduces a goal with its own subject: Herr Ali kocht Suppe, damit die Gäste satt werden. The verb of the damit-clause stands at the end, like after weil. With the same subject um … zu is better; with two different subjects only damit works. A damit-clause usually has no wollen or sollen. damit as a connector (so that, verb at the end) is not the da-word damit (with it, verb in position 2).

mistake.why: Two different subjects (Herr Ali, die Gäste): use damit. um … zu is only for the same person.

cards.title: Before we start: from 'um … zu' to 'damit die Gäste …'
cards.body: Herr Ali owns the restaurant „Zum Löwen“, and he hates throwing food away. You know how to say a goal when one person acts: Ich koche Suppe, um Reste zu verwenden. But what if the goal is for somebody else, or for the food itself? Today you meet damit.
steps: You already know: Ich koche Suppe, um Reste zu verwenden.: um … zu with one person.
New today: Ich koche Suppe, damit weniger im Müll landet.: damit, with a new subject and the verb at the end.
By the end you can: give a goal for another person with damit, and choose between um … zu and damit.

examples.de: Ich koche Suppe, um Reste zu verwenden.
examples.en: I cook soup in order to use up leftovers.
examples.why: You know this: one person, um … zu.

examples.de: Ich koche Suppe, damit weniger im Müll landet.
examples.en: I cook soup so that less ends up in the bin.
examples.why: New today: damit, with the verb at the end.

cards.more: A goal is like a delivery. With um … zu you deliver to yourself: the person who cooks also gets the result. With damit the parcel goes to somebody else, so you must name the receiver with a new subject: die Gäste, wir, es, du. The new subject is the big difference, and it sends the verb to the end, as after weil. Keep that image: a new receiver, a new subject, the verb at the end.

cards.title: Herr Ali's Resteteller
cards.body: Saturday in the kitchen of „Zum Löwen“. Herr Ali explains a new idea to Leon, and he says du to him. Look for damit in the answers and find the verb: it is always the last word of its part.
cards.lead: A new connector appears in the kitchen. Read the dialogue and watch what damit does to the word order: the verb moves to the end, and a new subject often follows right after damit.

examples.de: Ab Montag gibt es einen Resteteller, damit wir weniger wegwerfen.
examples.en: From Monday there is a leftovers plate, so that we throw away less.

examples.de: Ich koche Suppe, damit die Gäste satt werden.
examples.en: I cook soup so that the guests get full.

examples.de: Dann schreibe ich eine Karte, damit alle den Resteteller sehen.
examples.en: Then I write a card so that everybody sees the leftovers plate.

deeper.text: A goal always lies in the future, but the damit-clause still uses the present tense: damit die Gäste satt werden, not damit die Gäste satt werden werden. The main sentence can be in any tense. The future with werden is understood, but it sounds heavy, so people leave it out and simply use the present.

example.de: Herr Ali hat Suppe gekocht, damit die Gäste satt werden.
example.en: Herr Ali has cooked soup so that the guests get full.

cards.more: Think of damit as a tiny arrow pointing at a result, and of the verb as the arrowhead at the very end. In every line of the dialogue the arrow starts at the comma and ends with a verb: wegwerfen, werden, bleibt, sehen. Between the comma and the verb you find a new person or thing: wir, die Gäste, nichts, alle. Read the six lines aloud, and each time find the arrowhead and the new subject.
steps: Herr Ali: Leon, ab Montag gibt es einen Resteteller für 6 Euro, damit wir weniger wegwerfen.
Leon: Gute Idee! Was kommt auf den Teller?
Herr Ali: Reste vom Wochenende: Gemüse, Reis, Brot. Ich koche Suppe, damit die Gäste satt werden.
Leon: Und das Brot von gestern?
Herr Ali: Das Brot nehme ich für die Suppe, damit nichts übrig bleibt.
Leon: Dann schreibe ich eine Karte, damit alle den Resteteller sehen.

cards.title: Two subjects: damit
cards.body: damit joins two parts with two different subjects. Herr Ali cooks, but the guests become full. The comma stands before damit, the second subject follows damit, and the verb of that part goes to the end, exactly as after weil.
cards.lead: In the kitchen scene a new person always appeared after damit. Here you look at that pattern closely and see why a second subject calls for damit and not for um … zu.

examples.de: Herr Ali kocht Suppe, damit die Gäste satt werden.
examples.en: Herr Ali cooks soup so that the guests get full.

examples.de: Ich gebe dir eine Dose, damit du die Reste mitnimmst.
examples.en: I give you a box so that you take the leftovers along.

examples.de: Leon schreibt die Karte, damit die Gäste den Resteteller sehen.
examples.en: Leon writes the card so that the guests see the leftovers plate.

deeper.text: damit and sodass both start a clause with the verb at the end, but they mean different things. sodass gives a result that has already happened: Es regnete, sodass wir nass wurden. damit gives an intention, a plan: Ich nehme einen Schirm mit, damit ich nicht nass werde. If you can still change the outcome, use damit. If it is a result, use sodass.

example.de: Ich nehme einen Schirm mit, damit ich nicht nass werde.
example.en: I take an umbrella along so that I do not get wet.

cards.more: Picture two people on a stage: the actor of the first part and the actor of the second. In Herr Ali kocht Suppe, damit die Gäste satt werden, the spotlight jumps from Herr Ali to die Gäste. Every time the spotlight jumps to a new person, damit is ready. And as after weil, the verb walks off the stage last. If you cannot name a second actor, you probably want um … zu instead.

cards.title: um … zu or damit?
cards.body: Same person in both parts: um … zu is the better choice. Two different persons: only damit works. With the same subject damit is possible, but it sounds heavier. Ask yourself first: who does the second thing?
cards.lead: You now have two ways to name a goal. This card gives you one question to decide between them, so that you never have to guess which pattern fits.

examples.de: Ich spare, um zu reisen.
examples.en: I save in order to travel.
examples.why: Same person: um … zu.

examples.de: Ich spare, damit meine Kinder später studieren.
examples.en: I save so that my children can study later.

examples.de: Ich nehme einen Schirm mit, damit ich nicht nass werde.
examples.en: I take an umbrella along so that I do not get wet.

deeper.text: With a negative goal both patterns work: Ich nehme einen Schirm mit, damit ich nicht nass werde, or Ich nehme einen Schirm mit, um nicht nass zu werden. In the second sentence nicht stands before the rest of the goal and before zu. In careful writing, such as letters and articles, people prefer um … zu when the subject stays the same.

example.de: Ich nehme einen Schirm mit, um nicht nass zu werden.
example.en: I take an umbrella along in order not to get wet.

cards.more: Think of a small decision tree with one question: Who does the second thing? If the answer is the same person, take the short road: um … zu, with no second subject. If the answer is another person, there is only one road: damit, with a new subject and the verb at the end. If you take the damit road with the same person, you do not make an error, you only take a longer way. Most speakers prefer the short road.

rows: Ich nehme einen Schirm mit, damit ich nicht nass werde.
Ich spare, damit meine Kinder später studieren.

cards.title: No modal verbs in the damit-clause
cards.body: damit already says so that something can or should happen. So you do not add wollen or sollen to a damit-clause. Use the plain verb: damit du es verstehst. kannst is possible, but it is heavy.
cards.lead: A typical learner mistake is to put a modal verb into the damit-clause, because English says so that you can. German packs that idea into damit itself, and this card shows how to keep the clause light.

examples.de: Ich erkläre es langsam, damit du es verstehst.
examples.en: I explain it slowly so that you understand it.

examples.de: Ich zeige dir das Rezept, damit du die Suppe auch kochst.
examples.en: I show you the recipe so that you can cook the soup too.

examples.de: Herr Ali schreibt das Datum auf die Dose, damit niemand es vergisst.
examples.en: Herr Ali writes the date on the box so that nobody forgets it.

deeper.text: Native speakers do use können in a damit-clause when ability is the real point: Der Tisch ist groß, damit alle essen können. This is correct, and you will hear it often. You do not need to produce it yet, because a plain verb nearly always works: Der Tisch ist groß, damit alle Platz haben. Wollen and sollen stay out in both cases.

example.de: Der Tisch ist groß, damit alle Platz haben.
example.en: The table is big so that everybody has room.

cards.more: Think of damit as a word that already contains a little helper: so that … may. Because the helper is inside, you must not hire a second one. Compare a sandwich that already has cheese: you do not add another slice of cheese on top. Say the plain verb and let damit do the work: damit nichts übrig bleibt, damit wir weniger wegwerfen. If your sentence feels long and heavy, a modal verb has probably crept in.

rows: damit du es verstehen kannst (possible, heavy)
so that nothing is left over
so that we throw away less

cards.title: damit or damit?
cards.body: The same word has two jobs. As a da-word it means with it, and the verb stays in position 2. As a connector it means so that, comes after a comma, and sends the verb to the end. Test: comma plus verb at the end means connector.
cards.lead: You met damit in B1 chapter 4 as a da-word: Ich putze damit. Now the same spelling has a second meaning. This card sets the two side by side, so that you can tell them apart at once.

examples.de: Ich putze den Tisch damit.
examples.en: I clean the table with it.
examples.why: da-word: with it, verb in position 2.

examples.de: Ich putze den Tisch, damit er sauber wird.
examples.en: I clean the table so that it becomes clean.
examples.why: connector: so that, verb at the end.

examples.de: Damit putzt du den Herd.
examples.en: You clean the stove with it.

deeper.text: Two questions lead to the two damit words. Womit? asks for the tool and gets the da-word: Womit putzt du den Tisch? – Damit! (with this). Wozu? asks for the goal and gets the connector, or um … zu: Wozu putzt du den Tisch? – Damit er sauber wird. So the question word tells you which damit you need.

example.de: Womit putzt du den Tisch?
example.en: What do you clean the table with?

cards.more: Think of two keys that look exactly the same but open different doors. The da-word key opens the door of things: a cloth, a knife, a box. You can point at the thing and say damit. The connector key opens the door of goals: so that something happens. You cannot point at it, because it is a plan. The comma is your label on the key: after the comma, with the verb at the end, you hold the connector key.

rows: Ich putze, damit es sauber wird.

cards.title: Planning less food waste
cards.body: In the WG and in Herr Ali's kitchen the goals are practical: store food well, cook smaller portions. Mix both patterns: um … zu when the same person acts, damit when somebody or something else gets the result.
cards.lead: Now both patterns work together. This card shows the WG fridge plan, where every action has a goal. Watch how each sentence chooses between um … zu and damit by asking who does the second thing.

examples.de: Wir frieren Brot ein, damit es nicht verdirbt.
examples.en: We freeze bread so that it does not go bad.

examples.de: Wir kochen kleinere Portionen, um weniger wegzuwerfen.
examples.en: We cook smaller portions in order to throw away less.

examples.de: Ben schreibt eine Liste, um nichts doppelt zu kaufen.
examples.en: Ben writes a list in order not to buy anything twice.

deeper.text: The Mindesthaltbarkeitsdatum, short MHD, is a best-before date, not a death date. Many foods are still good after it. A different label, zu verbrauchen bis, is a use-by date, for example on raw mince or fish, and there the date really matters. Learn the two labels, and you will throw away much less.

example.de: Viele Lebensmittel sind auch nach dem Datum noch gut.
example.en: Many foods are still good after the date.

cards.more: Imagine the fridge door in the WG with four small notes, one per problem: bread, portions, fruit, shopping. Each note has two parts: what we do, and what for. When the goal belongs to the doer, the second part is short: um … zu. When the goal belongs to somebody else, or to the food, the second part has its own subject: damit. Walk past the notes and ask each time: who gets the result?

lessons.title: Zehn Umwelttipps
lessons.goal: Give and understand environmental tips with the patterns you know, add a reason with um … zu or damit, and say which bin something goes into.

grammar.topic: Tips and reasons: patterns you already know
grammar.point: No new grammar. A tip can be an Imperativ (Nimm …! Nehmt …!), Man sollte …, Am besten + verb, Es ist besser, … zu … or Vergiss nicht, … zu …. After vergessen the zu stands inside a separable verb: zurückzubringen. A reason follows with um … zu (same person) or damit (new subject, verb at the end).
grammar.oneLine: Bring Flaschen zurück, um das Pfand zu bekommen.

mistake.why: After vergessen: zu + infinitive, and with a separable verb zu goes inside the verb.

terms.meaning: the command form: Trenn den Müll! Bringt die Flaschen zurück!
a short piece of advice, often with a reason: Schalt das Licht aus, um Strom zu sparen.
a deposit you pay on a bottle and get back when you return it

cards.title: Before we start: from 'Du solltest …' to 'Trenn den Müll, damit …'
cards.body: In the WG, rubbish is a daily topic, and everybody has advice for everybody. You already know how to advise: Du solltest dich bewerben. Today no new grammar comes. You put together what you know, tips, goals with um … zu and damit, and you add the German bins.
steps: You already know: Du solltest dich bewerben.: advice with sollte from B1 chapter 4.
New today: Bring Flaschen zurück, um das Pfand zu bekommen.: a tip with a reason, plus the waste bins.
By the end you can: give and understand ten typical environmental tips, and say which bin something goes into.

examples.de: Du solltest dich bewerben.
examples.en: You should apply.
examples.why: You know this: advice with sollte.

examples.de: Bring Flaschen zurück, um das Pfand zu bekommen.
examples.en: Bring bottles back in order to get the deposit.
examples.why: New today: a tip with a reason.

cards.more: Think of a tip as a small gift in two layers. The outer layer is the advice itself: Bring Flaschen zurück. The inner layer is the reason that makes people want to follow it: um das Pfand zu bekommen. A tip without the inner layer works too, but with it people remember it better. You already own both layers. Today you only learn to wrap them together and to choose the right bin.

cards.title: Ben's Mülltrennung chaos
cards.body: Ben has put a pizza box into the yellow bin. Mira explains why that is wrong, and what goes where. The dialogue uses tips, um … zu and damit: no new grammar, only new words for waste.
cards.lead: A small disaster in the kitchen shows how waste separation works. Read the dialogue and notice how Mira gives her advice: she corrects, explains and gives a reason in the same breath.

examples.de: Der Karton ist fettig, er kommt in den Restmüll.
examples.en: The box is greasy, it goes into the general waste.

examples.de: Wir trennen den Müll, um Papier und Glas zu recyceln.
examples.en: We separate the waste in order to recycle paper and glass.

examples.de: Ich mache eine Liste, damit du nichts vergisst.
examples.en: I make a list so that you forget nothing.

deeper.text: Where something goes is a Wohin? question, so the accusative follows: in den Restmüll, in die Tonne, in das Altpapier. A very natural verb is gehören: Fettiger Karton gehört in den Restmüll. It says where something belongs, and it is shorter than a long explanation. You can use it for bins, but also for the kitchen cupboard or the bookshelf.

example.de: Fettiger Karton gehört in den Restmüll.
example.en: Greasy cardboard belongs in the general waste.

cards.more: Imagine the Mülltrennung as the sorting room of a post office. Every object arrives like a letter, and it must go into the right box. Ben simply read the address wrongly. Mira acts like the post office clerk: she looks at the object, names the right box, and adds a reason, so that Ben learns the rule and not only the answer. When you see a dialogue about rules, look for these three moves: look, name, explain.
steps: Ben: Fertig! Ich habe den Pizzakarton in die gelbe Tonne geworfen.
Mira: Nein, Ben! Der Karton ist fettig. Er kommt in den Restmüll.
Ben: Und das Papier hier?
Mira: Sauberes Papier kommt in die blaue Tonne. Wir trennen den Müll, um Papier und Glas zu recyceln.
Ben: Mülltrennung ist nicht so einfach!
Mira: Keine Sorge, ich mache eine Liste, damit du nichts vergisst.

cards.title: Which bin?
cards.body: Germany separates waste into bins. In many towns: yellow is for packaging, blue for paper, brown for organic waste, grey or black for general waste. Glass goes to the bottle bank, sorted by colour. The colours differ from town to town.
cards.lead: The pizza box showed that a wrong bin is easy. This card gives you the standard system in one table, so that you can name the right bin for the most common things.

examples.de: Das Altpapier kommt in die blaue Tonne.
examples.en: The waste paper goes into the blue bin.

examples.de: Obstreste kommen in die Biotonne.
examples.en: Fruit scraps go into the organic bin.

examples.de: Das Altglas bringe ich zum Glascontainer.
examples.en: I take the waste glass to the bottle bank.

deeper.text: A practical rule for the pizza box: food on it means Restmüll, a clean piece of paper means Altpapier. So a clean lid can go into the blue bin, and the greasy bottom into the general waste. The same logic works for other paper: a dirty napkin is not paper for recycling. When in doubt, ask whether the object is clean and what it is made of.

example.de: Der saubere Deckel kommt ins Altpapier, der fettige Boden in den Restmüll.
example.en: The clean lid goes into the waste paper, the greasy bottom into the general waste.

cards.more: Learn the bins as four colour pairs: gelb with Verpackung, blau with Papier, braun with Bio, grau or schwarz with Rest. Then every new object becomes two quick questions: What is it made of? Is it clean? A glass jar without deposit goes to the Glascontainer, a milk carton to the yellow bin. In a new town, look at the lids or at the leaflet of the city, because colours and names can change.

cards.title: Tip patterns
cards.body: Five patterns carry almost every tip. Choose by tone: the Imperativ is direct and friendly, Man sollte is general, Am besten opens a best-choice tip. Es ist besser and Vergiss nicht both use zu + infinitive.
cards.lead: Mira's list for Ben is full of tips. All of them are built from the same few patterns, which you know from earlier lessons. This card collects them in one place, so you can pick the right tone.

examples.de: Am besten kaufst du auf dem Markt ein.
examples.en: It is best to shop at the market.

examples.de: Es ist besser, Leitungswasser zu trinken.
examples.en: It is better to drink tap water.

examples.de: Vergiss nicht, die Flaschen zurückzubringen.
examples.en: Don't forget to bring the bottles back.

deeper.text: Am besten is a fixed opener that fills position 1, so the verb comes second: Am besten kaufst du … It turns an order into friendly advice, because it says my best idea is …. Compare Du musst Flaschen zurückbringen, which sounds like a rule, with Am besten bringst du die Flaschen zurück, which sounds like a good tip between friends. It is the most natural way to start a tip.

example.de: Am besten bringst du die Flaschen zurück.
example.en: It is best to bring the bottles back.

cards.more: Think of a volume dial for tips. Turn it up and you get the Imperativ: Nimm eine Tasche mit! Short, direct, friendly between flatmates. A little lower sits Vergiss nicht, … zu …, a reminder. Lower still are Am besten …, Man sollte … and Es ist besser, … zu …, which sound like advice, not like a command. When you tell a friend what to do, pick the setting that fits your tone, and the person will feel respected.

rows: Nimm eine Tasche mit! Nehmt Dosen mit!
Am besten kaufst du auf dem Markt ein.
Es ist besser, Leitungswasser zu trinken.

cards.title: Tips with a reason
cards.body: A tip is stronger with a reason. Use um … zu when the person you advise acts for themselves. Use damit when the effect is for others or for things. These are the two patterns from lessons 4 and 5, now inside tips.
cards.lead: A bare order is easy to ignore, but an order with a reason is easier to follow. This card adds the goal to the tip, and you see how um … zu and damit fit behind an imperative.

examples.de: Schalt das Licht aus, um Strom zu sparen.
examples.en: Switch off the light in order to save electricity.

examples.de: Kauft regionales Obst, damit es keine langen Transportwege gibt.
examples.en: Buy regional fruit so that there are no long transport routes.

examples.de: Bring Flaschen zurück, um das Pfand zu bekommen.
examples.en: Bring bottles back in order to get the deposit.

deeper.text: The imperative has three common forms. With du, the ending -st disappears: du trennst becomes Trenn!, and a verb with e → i becomes Nimm!, Gib!. With ihr, you keep the ending -t, and many learners forget it: Trennt! Bringt! Kauft! With Sie the verb comes first and Sie follows: Trennen Sie! A reminder note in the WG usually uses du or ihr.

example.de: Trennt den Müll und bringt die Flaschen zurück!
example.en: Separate the waste and bring the bottles back!

cards.more: Picture a tip sandwich. The first slice is the advice, Schalt das Licht aus. The second slice is the reason, um Strom zu sparen. A sandwich with only one slice is dry. If you give the tip to one person who also benefits, the filling is um … zu. If the benefit goes to somebody else, to the town or to the food, the filling is damit with a new subject. Taste the sentence aloud: does the reason belong to the doer?

rows: Schalt das Licht aus, um Strom zu sparen.
Kauft regionales Obst, damit es keine langen Transportwege gibt.

cards.title: The WG fridge list
cards.body: On the fridge in the WG hangs a list with ten environmental tips. Every tip uses a pattern from the last cards, and most give a reason with um … zu or damit. Read them as a model for your own tips.
cards.lead: Now everything comes together. The WG has written its own ten tips and stuck them on the fridge. Use them as a model, and notice how each one chooses its pattern and its reason.

examples.de: Man sollte Reste einfrieren, damit sie nicht verderben.
examples.en: You should freeze leftovers so that they do not go bad.

examples.de: Vergiss nicht, alte Batterien richtig zu entsorgen.
examples.en: Don't forget to dispose of old batteries properly.

examples.de: Es ist besser, kurz zu duschen.
examples.en: It is better to shower briefly.

deeper.text: On public signs the tone changes: instead of du you read Sie or a plain infinitive, often with Bitte. Bitte trennen Sie den Müll. or Bitte Müll trennen. You will see such signs in stairwells, parks and stations. Among flatmates, du is normal, but in a stairwell of a big house a sign with Sie sounds more neutral and polite.

example.de: Bitte trennen Sie den Müll.
example.en: Please separate your waste.

cards.more: Imagine you must write the ten tips again for a new flatmate, but you may only change the pattern. Start with a plain imperative. Then say the same tip with Am besten. Then say it as Man sollte. You will see that the content stays the same, only the tone changes. This is the best way to own the five patterns: practise one tip in three tones. Choose the tone to match who you talk to.
steps: 1. Nimm immer eine Stofftasche mit, um Plastiktüten zu vermeiden.
2. Trink Leitungswasser, um Geld zu sparen.
3. Trennt den Müll, um Papier und Glas zu recyceln.
4. Bring Flaschen zurück, um das Pfand zu bekommen.
5. Kauft regionales Obst, damit es keine langen Transportwege gibt.
6. Am besten planst du das Essen, um weniger wegzuwerfen.
7. Man sollte Reste einfrieren, damit sie nicht verderben.
8. Schalt das Licht aus, um Strom zu sparen.
9. Vergiss nicht, alte Batterien richtig zu entsorgen.
10. Es ist besser, kurz zu duschen.

cards.title: D-A-CH: other places, other rules
cards.body: Rules differ. In most Swiss municipalities you pay for a special rubbish bag, the Sackgebühr: more waste costs more money. Pfand and recycling rules also differ in Österreich and der Schweiz. In a new place, always ask.
cards.lead: Waste rules are not the same in all German-speaking countries. This last card shows three differences, so that you are not surprised in Wien or Zürich, and so you know what to ask.

examples.de: In den meisten Gemeinden der Schweiz zahlt man eine Sackgebühr.
examples.en: In most municipalities in Switzerland you pay a bag fee.

examples.de: In Österreich gelten für Pfand und Recycling andere Regeln.
examples.en: In Austria other rules apply to deposit and recycling.

examples.de: Am besten fragst du in einer neuen Stadt nach den Regeln.
examples.en: In a new town it is best to ask about the rules.

deeper.text: Even the word for rubbish changes. In Germany you say Müll and Mülleimer. In Switzerland people say Kehricht, as in Kehrichtsack. In Austria, especially in Wien, you often hear Mist and Mistkübel for the bin. Mira, who comes from Wien, still says Mistkübel at home. All three words are understood, but Müll is the safest choice everywhere.

example.de: In Wien heißt der Mülleimer oft Mistkübel.
example.en: In Vienna the rubbish bin is often called Mistkübel.

cards.more: Think of waste rules as a language with three dialects. The basic grammar is the same: separate, recycle, bring things back. But each dialect has its own words and its own prices. In Switzerland the bag costs money, so people think twice before filling it. In Austria the rules for deposit and recycling work differently. Always keep one habit: when you move, ask how the town does it.
